What changed between the proposed and the adopted budget

Council adopted the FY 2026-27 budget on August 12, 2026 (9-2; Mayor Watson and CM Duchen against). The two analysis files describe the July PROPOSED budget. This note records what moved, from the City's adoption press release and Community Impact's coverage, so the video uses adopted figures. Checked 2026-09-12. The adopted budget document itself was not yet posted.

ItemProposed (July)Adopted (Aug 12)
Total budget$6,625.3 M$6.63 B (no material change)
General Fund$1,538.9 M (+3.6%)about $1.5 B (+3.6%)
Tax rate per $100$0.579530$0.579948
Median non-senior homestead value$484,907$471,603 (certified roll)
City tax bill on that home$2,248.15 (+$173.87, +8.4%)about $2,190 (+$113.76, +5.5%)
Utility and fee increase, typical ratepayer$172.08 / yr$172.08 / yr (unchanged)
Combined typical household increase$345.95 / yr$285.84 / yr ($23.82 / mo)
Total typical household cost$6,012.79 / yrabout $5,950 / yr

The rate went UP slightly and the bill increase went DOWN: the certified roll came in with a lower median value than the July estimate, so the same voter-approval-cap revenue is spread over a smaller base. The rate is the maximum allowed without an election.

Council amendments (from the press release)

  • $1.4 M for a new Office of Joint Emergency Communications (passed 6-2-3).
  • $33 M of non-voter-approved debt for capital safety improvements: active mobility, traffic calming, and about $3 M for Animal Services facilities (Community Impact reports the debt figure as $35 M).
  • $300 K more for Homeless Strategies and Operations staffing and shelter management.
  • $500 K for the Violet KeepSafe Storage program.
  • $114,521 cut from consultant spending in Housing and Planning.
  • Parks maintenance equipment and a downtown drink-spiking safety program (amounts not stated).

City of Austin FY 2026-27 Proposed Budget, Volume I: Analysis

Source: City of Austin FY 2026-27 Proposed Budget, Volume I (481 pages, an image-only "Print to PDF" scan, OCR'd 2026-09-11; the text is in ocr/AustinProposedBuget2026vol1.ocr.txt). Page numbers below are the printed page numbers, which match the PDF page index.

Volume I covers the City Manager's message, the Budget in Brief, the FY 2028 planned budget and five-year forecast, the Citywide Strategic Plan update, and one section per department (KPIs, milestones, budget by fund and program, significant changes). Volume II (fund summaries, CIP detail) was not analyzed.

1. The headline numbers

Sources: pp. 13-14, 31, 40, 45, 51-53.

The single most important sentence in the document is on p. 77: the tax base shrank. Taxable value fell 3.4% (about $550 M of that from the senior/disabled exemption rising to $204,000), and new construction added only $3.2 B, described as "the continuing lull in development activity across the City." The rate goes up 10.6% mostly to hold revenue flat against a falling base, plus a larger debt-service rate. Homeowners still see an 8.4% bill increase even though the median home lost value.

2. Where the money goes (all funds, $6.6 B)

Austin Energy 30%, General Fund 22%, Austin Water 13%, internal services 8%, Aviation 7%, GO debt service 5%, Transportation and Public Works 4%, Convention Center 3%, Resource Recovery 2%, Watershed 2% (p. 30).

Three departments account for more than half the citywide increase (p. 31):

  • Austin Energy +$62.6 M (+3.1%): debt service, compensation, ERCOT transmission.
  • Aviation +$62.1 M (+13.9%): expansion program, 25 new positions for Concourse M readiness.
  • Austin Water +$37.5 M (+4.3%): capital plan and 30 new positions.

Debt retirement funds jump 18.6% to $1,020.5 M and are planned to rise another 18.1% in FY 2028 (pp. 31, 76). Debt is the fastest-growing line in the budget.

3. General Fund: what changed

Public safety (police, fire, EMS) is 64.7% of the General Fund, $994.6 M (p. 33).

The Homeless / Social Services swing is mostly an accounting realignment: $19.4 M of emergency-shelter contracts moved from the grants line into the Homeless Strategy Office and Public Health budgets, "no net change in total funding" (p. 36, p. 330). The real cuts to third-party social service providers total $8.0 M in FY 2027 (p. 33), with another $8.8 M planned for FY 2028 (p. 77).

The budget nets $16.1 M of new investments against $13.3 M of reductions and reallocations (p. 33). Notable items (pp. 34-37):

  • Fire: +$6.0 M overtime to keep four-person staffing; $1.5 M reallocated from academy instructors back to the field.
  • Police: sworn headcount flat at 1,819; a 5% base wage step under the meet-and-confer contract costs $11.7 M; one civilian recruiting position; 17 IT positions transferred out to Technology Services.
  • Homelessness: $3 M ongoing for the Marshalling Yard shelter; $2 M more for permanent supportive housing services; $7.8 M total for local housing vouchers across three funds.
  • Parks: +$1.2 M for parkland and refurbished pools; $400 K saved by moving adult sports leagues to a rental model.
  • Library: five positions and $1.1 M one-time for the Austin History Center campus.
  • Public Health: 12 immunization-clinic positions moved from grant funding to the General Fund; Summer Youth Employment support to Travis County ended ($652 K reallocated); STI/HIV lab work outsourced.
  • Auditor: $1.5 M for a citywide efficiency audit.
  • Technology Services: $5.8 M saved through "ONE-ATS," the IT centralization that pulls positions in from Austin Energy (35), Development Services (22), Police (17) and others with no layoffs.

4. The structural problem, in the City's own words

Since the state capped property-tax revenue growth at 3.5% in FY 2021, staff have warned that the General Fund cannot stay balanced without flattening costs or finding new revenue (p. 81). The FY 2027 budget balances through ONE-ATS savings and the grant cuts. The FY 2028 planned budget balances only by:

  • assuming no wage adjustment for civilian staff in FY 2028, and
  • cutting social service grants a further $8.8 M (p. 77).

Even so, reserves are projected at 16.4% of ongoing spend in FY 2028, $9.9 M below the 17% policy floor. Small surpluses in FY 2029-31 depend on "significant further anticipated savings" from ONE-ATS that are not yet identified.

Five-year General Fund outlook (p. 81): $1,538.9 M (FY27), $1,590.7 M (FY28), $1,643.5 M, $1,692.8 M, $1,753.1 M (FY31). Revenue assumptions: taxable value +1% FY28, +2% FY29, +3% after; sales tax +2.5% then +3%/yr; voter-approval rate adopted every year.

5. Pay, benefits, pensions

  • Civilian raise 3.0% ($35.4 M citywide, $7.1 M General Fund), down from four straight years of 4%. Living wage moves $22.05 to $22.15 (p. 40).
  • Police 5.0% (contract), Fire 3.0% ($4.4 M, new four-year contract Dec 2025), EMS placeholder pending negotiation.
  • Health insurance: PPO premiums rise for the first time in several years ($30 to $40 employee-only); City contribution to the benefits fund up $20.9 M to $281.4 M (p. 41).
  • Pension contributions total $340.3 M. Unfunded liabilities: COAERS $2,294 M (63.1% funded), Police $790 M (59.7%), Fire $349.5 M (76.9%) (p. 43). Fitch restored the AAA GO rating in 2025 after the reforms.
  • $19.6 M is set aside for a citywide compensation market study.

6. Utility rates and fees, typical household

Austin Energy's 5% base-rate increase is masked by a lower Power Supply Adjustment, so the total bill rises only 3.1%; the Regulatory (ERCOT transmission) charge alone jumps 34% (p. 48). Austin Water's wastewater volume charge rises 12% (p. 50). Austin Water is the biggest household cost driver over the forecast, and it is adding 200 FTEs by FY 2031 (p. 95).

Utility transfers to the General Fund are $205.1 M (13.1% of GF revenue) and are projected to grow 5% a year, taking a rising share of the General Fund as the property tax cap bites (pp. 77-80).

7. The development slowdown shows up everywhere

  • Development Services Fund is in deficit: fund balance -$18.2 M at end FY 2026, -$22.8 M at end FY 2027, not back to zero until after FY 2031. Hiring freeze, 10 positions eliminated, 30 FTEs net reduction (pp. 101-102, 240).
  • Right-of-way permit revenue in Transportation down $4.0 M "as a result of a slowdown in development activity" (p. 104).
  • Planning zoning-application revenue down $476 K (p. 394).
  • Short-term rental licensing revenue down $0.8 M (renewal moved to biennial).
  • TXP economic forecast: MSA job growth 1.3% in 2026, 1.8% in 2027; April median home price $530 K, down from $640 K in 2022; office construction pipeline shrinking to 756 K sq ft; apartment rents down 6.5% over 12 months (pp. 66-73).
  • Sales tax: FY 2025 grew only 0.4%; FY 2026 estimated $384.6 M (+4.9%, inflation-driven); FY 2027 budgeted $394.3 M (+2.5%) (p. 55).

8. Capital

  • New CIP appropriations $6.2 B; FY 2027 spend plan $4.3 B; five-year plan $15.1 B, of which 79% is Austin Energy, Austin Water and Aviation (pp. 59, 112).
  • Funding of new appropriations: utility commercial paper 39.8%, airport revenue bonds 24.6%, current revenue 14.7%, other debt 13.1%, grants 2.8%, GO debt 1.5%.
  • Voter-approved bond programs are 68% spent overall (p. 61). 2018 Prop A housing 97%; 2018 Prop B libraries/museums 50%; 2020 mobility bond 57%; 2022 Prop A housing 32%.
  • Largest FY 2027 spend plans: Aviation $1.09 B, Austin Energy $1.01 B, Austin Water $652 M, Convention Center $650 M, Transportation and Public Works $267 M, Financial Services (facilities) $161 M, Fleet $89 M, Housing $83 M, Watershed $78 M (p. 62).
  • New operating costs from completed capital: 65 FTEs for facilities at the airport, the Public Safety HQ, Grove Boulevard and University Park; $1.1 M asphalt for expanded streets; $1.0 M for new parkland (p. 60).

9. Departments most relevant to planning and mapping work

Planning ($14.1 M, 100% General Fund, p. 389-394). Three positions added (historic preservation planner, demographer, commissions support), funded by cutting temporary staff. FY 2027 milestones: new zoning tools for mixed-use and missing-middle housing; comprehensive update of the Great Streets Plan. FY 2028: publish the draft Imagine Austin comprehensive plan update and adopt it; 10-year update of the East Austin Historic Resource Survey. New KPI: share of the city covered by area-focused planning in the last 10 years, target 17% rising to 24%.

Housing ($56.3 M all funds, p. 332-337). $2.1 M ongoing for local vouchers; two monitoring positions. The Homestead Preservation TIF fund spends $27.5 M in FY 2027 then drops to $13.0 M in FY 2028. KPI to watch: renter households helped with rental assistance falls from 3,422 (FY 2026 estimate) to a target of 300, and the Affordable Housing Inventory completions target is 2,335 units.

Homeless Strategies and Operations ($59.0 M, p. 325-330). Now operates City-owned shelters directly ($22.4 M moved in-house); 38 FTEs. New KPIs for shelter utilization (85%), exits to permanent housing (30% from shelter, 70% from rapid rehousing), and encampment request response (8 days, then 5). A GIS-linked 311 encampment tool is a FY 2028 milestone.

Transportation and Public Works ($249.2 M, p. 449-459). Revenue flat, TUF unchanged this year and +$1.10 in FY 2028. Sidewalk and Urban Trails operating program cut from $9.6 M to $6.7 M while General Maintenance rises $3.9 M. KPIs: 68% of lane miles fair or better vs 80% target; 42% of sidewalks functionally acceptable; 25.7% of the All Ages and Abilities bikeway network built; 319 traffic deaths and serious injuries estimated in FY 2026 against a Vision Zero target of 0. Milestone: quantify the maintenance funding gap for streets, bridges, sidewalks and signals and propose a lifecycle funding strategy. The 2016/2018/2020 mobility bonds are to be completed by FY 2028.

Watershed Protection ($133.9 M, Drainage Utility Fund, p. 469-475). Drainage charge +6.2% now and +22% more by FY 2031, funding a Storm Drain Rehabilitation Program, 18 positions now and 32 more later, and larger transfers to capital. Fund balance thin ($11-17 M). KPI on properties with reduced flood risk drops from 177 to 40 next year as the big projects finish; milestones are the Oak Acres and Del Curto flood-risk projects and a study of how much lost stormwater infiltration can be mitigated.

Development Services ($113.2 M, p. 238-245). Graffiti Abatement Program made permanent (7 positions); demolition backlog funded; residential permit fee increases capped at 10% with the General Fund covering the gap ($2.5 M). Milestones: emergency-demolition process, vacant-structure framework, adoption of the 2027 international codes, a simplified fee schedule.

10. Things to be careful about

  • The document is a scan. OCR dropped occasional lines, especially light-blue text and bullet leaders. Every number above was taken from a table row or a sentence that OCR'd cleanly, and the pages carrying the key figures (16, 77, 81) were checked against the page image. Treat single-figure claims as "read from OCR" until confirmed in the PDF.
  • The FTE total is stated two ways: the narrative says 16,767 FTEs and +225 (p. 39), the table says 16,787 and +245 (p. 40). The table is the one that adds up.
  • Property tax figures are estimates: certified appraisal rolls had not arrived when the budget went to print (p. 14, p. 52 footnote). The rate, the median value and the bill will all move.
  • Vehicle Rental Tax and the 2-cent venue hotel tax expire in FY 2030 as the Palmer / original convention center debt retires (p. 82), a $46 M revenue drop for the Convention Center fund that the forecast already absorbs.

Possible follow-ups (not started)

  • Pull the Volume II five-year CIP spend plan into a table by council district for the Transportation and Watershed projects.
  • OCR Volume II with the same script (ocr/ocr_pdf.py, about 20 minutes).

City of Austin FY 2026-27 Proposed Budget, Volume II: Analysis

Source: City of Austin FY 2026-27 Proposed Budget, Volume II (661 pages, an image-only scan, OCR'd 2026-09-11). Text is in ocr/AustinProposedBuget2026vol2.ocr.txt; the landscape tables (CIP plan pp. 162-343 and fee schedule pp. 390-653) were re-OCR'd rotated into ocr/AustinProposedBuget2026vol2.cip-rotated.ocr.txt and ocr/AustinProposedBuget2026vol2.fees-rotated.ocr.txt. Page numbers are printed page numbers. Companion to ANALYSIS-vol1.md.

Volume II is the supporting detail behind Volume I: a ledger for every budgeted fund (pp. 10-145), grants (146-150), donation funds (151-154), the one-time reserve appropriations (155), the five-year Capital Improvement Program spend plan by department (156-343), the personnel table (344-345), financial policies (346-362), debt position and bond schedules (363-381), the budget calendar (382-383), the adopting ordinances (384-389), and the fee schedule (390-653).

1. What Volume II adds to the Volume I story

  • The General Fund stops cash-funding capital. Transfers out of the General Fund to capital funds (facilities $2.9 M, library $2.0 M, parks $1.0 M, general government $2.1 M) and to the Housing Trust Fund ($8.8 M) all drop to zero in FY 2027. Total General Fund transfers out fall from $36.6 M to $29.1 M to $25.0 M planned (p. 34).
  • FY 2026 was propped up by one-time money that is now gone. A $14.1 M draw from the Budget Stabilization Reserve and a $1.5 M transfer from Planning's capital fund were revenue in FY 2026; neither recurs (p. 33). Sales tax is estimated to beat the FY 2026 budget by $25.3 M ($384.6 M vs. $359.4 M), which is what made this year's books close.
  • The utility transfers keep rising. Austin Energy's General Fund transfer goes from $139 M to $147 M to $151 M planned; Austin Water's from $54.8 M to $58.1 M to $62.9 M (p. 33).
  • The FTE total is 16,767.02, which settles the discrepancy in Volume I: the narrative was right and the Volume I summary table (16,787) was wrong (p. 345).
  • Federal revenue in the General Fund is zero for FY 2027 after $1.25 M in FY 2025 (p. 33).

5. Transportation and Public Works: the bond pipeline ends in FY 2028

Bond-funded spending falls off a cliff after two years. Streets-capacity bond spending goes $68.4 M (FY27), $72.9 M, $34.4 M, $9.4 M, $5.9 M. Sidewalk bond spending goes $12.0 M, $4.3 M, $0.15 M, then nothing. Trails bond spending goes $21.0 M, $18.8 M, $1.2 M, $0.6 M. The FY 2026 sidewalk line is literally labeled "Capital Stop-Gap Sidewalk Funding" ($1.58 M) plus "remaining quarter cent" ($1.04 M) (pp. 314-327). This is the capital side of the Volume I milestone to "identify maintenance budget gaps and develop a long-term funding strategy." Authorized-but-unissued GO bonds stand at $1.03 B, including $340 M transportation and $239 M mobility (p. 365), and GO debt service falls every year from $270 M as old bonds roll off (p. 373), so there is room for a new bond program.

What is actually funded:

  • I-35 Cap and Stitch design integration: $23.7 M other debt in FY27-28 plus $10 M and $35.7 M other GO in FY27-28, about $69 M total (pp. 305-306). The single largest non-utility line in the plan.
  • 2016 corridor program, still spending: Burnet Road segments C2/C3/C4 ($21.6 M in FY27 alone), North Lamar (three segments plus a Howard Lane contraflow bus lane), South Lamar (two segments through FY30), William Cannon, Slaughter Lane, Airport Boulevard, East MLK/FM 969 ($6.1 M FY27), South Pleasant Valley, Spicewood Springs ($8.5 M), Lakeline Boulevard, West Rundberg extension (p. 317).
  • 2020 bond: Congress Avenue urban design $7 M, $9 M, $4 M (FY27-29); substandard streets Ross Road ($12.0 M FY27) and Johnny Morris Road (through FY31); sidewalks phase 3; Vision Zero intersection projects; local transit enhancements (pp. 315, 319, 321).
  • Urban trails: Bergstrom Spur (Central $5.2 M + $10.3 M, West $1.4 M + $1.5 M + grants $4.1 M, East $2.1 M), Walnut Creek Trail IH-35 to Southern Walnut Creek ($6.5 M), Shoal Creek Trail at FM 2222 underpass ($2.5 M), Country Club Creek Trail ($3.6 M), MoKan Trail Boggy Creek bridge, Red Line Trail segments, Northern Walnut Creek Trail grants $5 M (pp. 325-326).
  • Bridges: Barton Springs Road bridge over Barton Creek ($28 M over five years), Redbud Trail bridge over Lady Bird Lake ($11.2 M FY27-30), Longhorn Dam multimodal (p. 306).
  • Safe Streets for All grants: $14.6 M federal in FY27 with $13.7 M bond match: protected intersections at 7th/Springdale, Oltorf/Burton, Burleson/Stassney and 7th/Shady Lane; Rutland/Parkfield roundabout; Cameron/Dessau corridor and lighting; a 2024 SS4A award of $2.6 M a year through FY30 (pp. 320-321).
  • Climate Pollution Reduction Grant: $13.8 M a year FY27-29, three measures, federal (p. 310).
  • Traffic signals: CAMPO grants of $7.0 M FY27 and $4.9 M FY28 for transit signal priority, detection and cameras; a Travis County arterial ILA $1.5 M (p. 323).
  • Street impact fees: about $3.6 M a year spread across 16 service areas, plus $2.2 M of traffic-impact fee in lieu (p. 309). Parent project for Austin Transit Partnership, $4.2 M FY27.
  • Parking fund projects: East Austin parking ($3.5 M FY27-29), West Campus benefit district, South Congress, Mueller (p. 311).
  • Seaholm area mobility $1 M, $2.5 M, $7.4 M FY27-29; Braker Lane Samsung to Dawes $5.7 M; TPW tree program $600 K a year (pp. 320, 322).

6. Watershed Protection: $321 M, 87% from the drainage charge

  • Flood risk reduction (pp. 330-335): Del Curto storm drain ($9.7 M FY27-29), Walnut Creek Oak Knoll ($7.1 M), Oak Acres Creek ($4.8 M), Little Walnut Creek Metric-to-Rutland ($3.8 M), Slaughter Creek Vassal Drive phases 1-3 ($10.4 M over five years), Walnut Creek North Acres ($7.2 M), East Bouldin Annie Street ($2.7 M), Barton Creek Oak Park ($7.3 M, mostly FY30-31), Boggy Creek MLK TOD stormwater conveyance ($8.8 M), a Red Bluff hotel public-private partnership ($7.3 M), a $6 M contribution to the CPSC/Austin Water detention project, and three dam modernizations (Northwest Park, Old Lampasas #3, Duval).
  • Waller Creek: tunnel sediment and debris removal ($6.1 M FY27-29), tunnel SCADA and outlet work, Waterloo Greenway 4th-12th ($4.3 M other GO + $1.2 M grant), Waller Creek District Waterloo Greenway parent account ($4 M + $4.9 M), the Confluence Link ($2.3 M), a $6 M land line for the district (pp. 332-337).
  • Mapping and data, which is directly relevant to GIS work: Atlas 14 floodplain mapping updates for eight watershed groups, $2.2 M in FY27 plus $617 K in grants (Onion, Williamson/Slaughter/South Boggy, Walnut/Boggy, Urban West north and south of the river, Gilleland/NE Colorado, Dry East/Carson/SE Colorado) (p. 338); citywide storm drain infrastructure modeling ($907 K, $3.6 M, $2.1 M, $3.5 M); a localized flood modeling pilot ($600 K); LiDAR acquisition ($300 K FY27); impervious cover planimetrics ($55 K to $295 K a year); a conveyance-system GIS; drainage charge GIS integration (p. 336).
  • Flood early warning system $800 K FY27; voluntary buyouts $300 K rising to $1 M a year (pp. 336-337).
  • Water quality: Buttermilk Creek ($15.8 M TWDB debt FY28-30 plus current revenue), Bartholomew Park retrofit ($3.3 M FY28), AARC/Rutherford ($6.5 M), Kealing Park green infrastructure ($1.1 M), West Austin Park retrofits ($2.1 M), Project Connect betterments ($8.9 M FY27-31), riparian restoration $450 K a year (p. 340).
  • Erosion: Williamson Creek tributaries, Walnut Creek Eubank and Wells Branch, Little Walnut Loyola/Dottie Jordan, Sunken Gardens ($4.2 M FY29) (p. 332).

Named deals include Cameron HiLine, Verbena Flats, 5901 Drowsy Willow, 5900 South Pleasant Valley, Bailey at Stassney, Manor Apartments, Crossroads, Waverly North, The Bloom at Lamar Square, Goodnight Ranch, Seabrook Square I and II, Johnny Limon Village, Ada Anderson Place, Sunday Village, Carver Townhomes, Prospect Heights, St. George's Court, South First Affordable. Current-revenue lines carry the voucher program ($3.1 M), rental development assistance ($5.8 M FY27-28), and developer-agreement money from the Grove, Plaza Saltillo TOD, Pilot Knob MUD, North Burnet Gateway and the Green Water Treatment Plant site ($400 K a year).

Streetscapes: Great Streets resource account $1.75 M, $2.5 M, $2.1 M in FY29-31, Great Streets light poles $1 M FY29, the Great Streets Plan update $414 K FY27, Downtown Refresh $150 K (pp. 284-285).

10. Ordinances and calendar (pp. 382-389)

  • Proposed budget filed July 10; Council work sessions July 22 to August 6; tax rate hearing and adoption August 12-14.
  • The fee ordinance waives fees for the usual co-sponsored events (SXSW, ACL-adjacent events, Trail of Lights, Pride, Juneteenth, etc.), for S.M.A.R.T. Housing, for childcare facilities (up to $250 K), and for density-bonus affordable projects (up to $250 K).

11. Fee schedule: development fees go up hard, residential is shielded

Volume I said residential permitting increases are capped at 10% with the General Fund covering the gap. The schedule shows what that cap does not cover (pp. 465-488 Development Services, 530-533 Planning, 550-563 Transportation, 564-571 Watershed):

  • Zoning and land use (Development Services Fund): regular rezoning $1,976 to $2,652 (+34%); PUD creation $18,589 to $23,704 (+28%); PUD amendment needing Commission approval +70%; zoning variances +53%; sign variance +51%; zoning interpretation appeal +54%; annexation and Council-reviewed MUD amendments $1,339 to $2,183 (+63%); MUD consent $10,039 to $13,537 (+35%); out-of-district service request +95%; site plan completeness check $836 to $2,786 (+233%); site plan environmental review +30%; drainage review +34%; temporary use permit $124 to $737 (+494%); mobile retail permit $82 to $491 (+500%); alcoholic beverage waiver +30%; subdivision fees +20% to +28%; short-term rental notification doubled. A few fall: site plan change-of-use exemption (-25%), general PUD amendment (-35%), preliminary plan extension (-51%), subdivision inspection intake (-6% to -8%).
  • Planning: the DB90 and ETOD fee-in-lieu for ownership units is recalibrated: 1-bedroom $201,900 to $136,900 (-32%), 2-bedroom -10%, 3-bedroom $497,800 to $606,299 (+22%), 4-bedroom +35%. MLK TOD density bonus $12 to $15 per bonus square foot. Historic: Certificate of Appropriateness $80 to $50, historic zoning application $810 to $500, landmark plaque +66%, residential outbuilding demolition $40 to $98, public hearing preparation fee eliminated. MUD/PID planning fees drop sharply (PID $101,045 to $14,276, out-of-district -87%) while administratively approved amendments jump ($1,605 to $8,286).
  • Transportation: nearly every development review fee rises 19% (consolidated site plan review $8,275 to $9,825; TIA scoping; MUD and PUD reviews); right-of-way permit applications +16% to +27%; traffic control plan review +35%; utility coordination case $4,195 to $5,873 (+40%); street and alley vacations $14,415 to $19,460 (+35%); completeness checks +130% to +218%. TIA reviews for large projects fall slightly (-2% to -4%).
  • Watershed: discharge permit fees flat; environmental reinspection -18%; the Regional Stormwater Management Program payment formula is restated with a 50% discount for developments over 50% affordable and a proportional discount for 10%-50% affordable.
  • Property tax exemptions (p. 634): homestead 20%; over-65 and disabled $204,000; disabled veterans $5,000 to $12,000 by rating, 100% for fully disabled; qualifying child-care facilities 100%; a list of roughly 130 historic landmarks receiving the partial exemption, with FY26 inspection pass/fail results (a handful show "Fail").

12. Handle with care

  • The CIP and fee tables were scanned in landscape and OCR'd after rotating. Project names and dollar figures on those pages are more error-prone than the portrait pages: expect a dropped digit or a "0" read as "o" here and there. Every figure above was cross-checked against a row total or a repeated value where possible.
  • Fee schedule rows print the old fee, the new fee and the percent change; where OCR mangled a number the percent change was used as the check.
  • The fund ledgers (pp. 10-145) were not all read; the General Fund, Support Services, Airport, Code, Development Services, Homeless, Housing, Parking, Transportation and Drainage funds were. Volume I already summarizes the rest.
  • The 200-page utility rate tariffs (pp. 572-633) were not analyzed.
